html:
A canal across upstate New York, built from 1817 to 1825, that joined the Great Lakes to the Atlantic. It ran about 584 kilometres from Buffalo on Lake Erie to Albany on the Hudson River, with dozens of locks to climb and descend.

Governor DeWitt Clinton pushed it through, and critics mocked it as "Clinton's Ditch". It was dug largely by hand, by local farmers and Irish immigrants, with almost no trained engineers.

It was a huge success:

  • Freight costs from the Midwest to the coast fell sharply, and travel times shrank from weeks to days.
  • Farmers in Ohio, Indiana and Michigan could sell grain to the East, which drew settlers west.
  • Towns along the route, such as Rochester, Syracuse and Buffalo, boomed.
  • New York City became the country's leading port and money centre, home of the New York Stock Exchange.

Its success set off a canal building craze in the United States, until railroads took over the traffic from the 1850s.
